summary: Defines DHCPv6 options used to boot a node from the network. They give the node the information needed to find and fetch its boot image. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A computer with no memory asks the network where to find what it needs to wake up.

questions: how does ipv6 network boot work
how to pass boot parameters over dhcpv6
subtitle: Four DHCPv6 options that tell a computer where to fetch its boot file and how to run it.

tldr.problem: A node that boots from the network rather than local storage needs to learn where its boot file is, how to download it and what parameters to pass, and DHCPv6 had no options for that.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5970 defines options for a boot file URL, boot file parameters, client architecture types and a network interface identifier, which the client requests from a DHCPv6 server.
tldr.outcome: The boot file URL option is mandatory for booting and the others are optional. The RFC also creates an IANA registry of processor architecture types.

today: RFC 5970 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its four option codes and the Processor Architecture Types registry are the ones the text itself describes.

sections.title: Network Boot with DHCPv6
sections.content:
Some nodes must boot over the network rather than from local storage. The RFC notes this helps where administrators maintain a large number of nodes, because all boot and configuration files can be served from a central server. A typical boot file is an operating system kernel or a boot-loader program.

The client firmware does two things: first it gets the information needed to download and execute the boot file, then it downloads and runs it. The information MUST include at least the server holding the files, the download protocol (for example HTTP or TFTP) and the path and name of the file. The server and client MAY also exchange parameters for the kernel or boot loader and information about the supported boot environment.
sections.eli5: First the computer asks where its instructions are kept. Then it goes there, picks them up and starts following them.

sections.title: The Boot File URL and Parameters Options
sections.content:
Option formats follow RFC 3315. The boot-file-url option is mandatory for booting, and all other options are optional.

The Boot File URL option (OPT_BOOTFILE_URL, code 59) is sent by the server and carries a URL for the boot file. The string MUST comply with STD 66 (RFC 3986) and is not NUL-terminated. If the host is an IPv6 address, it MUST be enclosed in square brackets. Clients that have DNS implementations SHOULD support domain names in the URL.

The Boot File Parameters option (OPT_BOOTFILE_PARAM, code 60) is sent by the server and holds several UTF-8 strings, each preceded by a 16-bit length. They work like command line arguments, for example naming the root file system of a kernel. When the firmware runs the boot file it MUST pass these parameters, in the order they appear.
sections.eli5: One option is the street address of the instructions. The other is a list of notes to take along, handed over in the same order they were written.

sections.title: Architecture and Interface Options
sections.content:
Two options give parity with DHCPv4 options in RFC 4578. The Client System Architecture Type option (OPTION_CLIENT_ARCH_TYPE, code 61) carries a list of 16-bit architecture types describing the client's pre-boot runtime environment. Its length MUST be an even number greater than zero. The client MAY send its supported types so the server can choose a suitable boot file, with the most preferred first. If the client used the option, the server SHOULD include it in reply, listing only types the client asked about, again in descending priority.

The Client Network Interface Identifier option (OPTION_NII, code 62) lets a client that supports the Universal Network Device Interface (UNDI) tell the server its level of support. It has a length of 3 and three one-octet fields, Type, Major and Minor, defined in RFC 4578. Valid values are maintained in the UEFI specification.
sections.eli5: The computer can say what kind of machine it is, so the server sends a program that fits it, and the best fit is listed first.

sections.title: Where Options May Appear and How Files Download
sections.content:
These options MUST NOT appear in DHCPv6 messages other than Solicit, Advertise, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reply. Their option codes MAY appear in the Option Request option in Solicit, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reconfigure messages.

The URL option places no constraint on the download protocol, other than that it can be written in a URL. The RFC strongly recommends that boot loaders implement HTTP at a minimum, and notes that for IPv6 this supersedes RFC 906, which recommended TFTP. For iSCSI booting, the functionality that RFC 4173 gave to a root path option is provided by the Boot File URL option instead.
sections.eli5: There are rules for which messages may carry these notes. The boot file itself can be fetched by any method that fits in an address, but the web is the one everyone should support.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned four option numbers from the DHCPv6 option space: 59 (OPT_BOOTFILE_URL), 60 (OPT_BOOTFILE_PARAM), 61 (OPTION_CLIENT_ARCH_TYPE) and 62 (OPTION_NII).

The RFC also creates a new registry called "Processor Architecture Types". Entries are a 16-bit integer in decimal plus a descriptive name, the initial values come from RFC 4578, and new values are assigned through Expert Review.
sections.eli5: The numbers 59 to 62 are reserved for these notes, and there is a public list of computer types that anyone can ask to add to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
On an untrusted network a rogue DHCPv6 server could send these options and point clients at a wrong URL. The boot would then fail or, worse, the client would boot the wrong operating system from a malicious file server. Clients SHOULD use DHCPv6 message authentication to prevent this.

DHCPv6 messages are unencrypted by default, so URLs can leak sensitive information such as a user name and password. The RFC strongly recommends not putting sensitive information in URLs on untrusted networks.

Securing the DHCPv6 exchange does not protect the download itself. The RFC recommends either HTTPS or TLS within HTTP to prevent spoofing, or boot-loader software that verifies signed boot images with a configurable signing key, so a malicious image can be detected and rejected.
sections.eli5: A trickster could hand out a fake address and the computer would wake up with the wrong instructions. So the computer should check who is talking and check the package it receives.
